summary: For learners aged 9–10: divide numbers up to 4 digits by a one-digit number using the short-division ('bus stop') method, grounded in place-value exchange, and interpret the remainder according to the context (round up, round down, keep as a remainder, or express as a fraction/decimal). The central insight is that the same calculation can yield different correct answers depending on the story, and that answers should be checked by multiplying back and against an estimate.
misconceptions: Mishandling the remainder carry — not moving it to the next place or adding it wrongly.
Interpreting the remainder wrongly for the context (rounding down when you must round up, e.g. minibuses).
Dropping a place when the digit is smaller than the divisor (not writing the 0 and carrying).
Not checking with multiplication, so errors persist.
Treating short division as digit-manipulation divorced from place value/sharing meaning.

activities.title: Share the columns: short division with place-value counters
steps: Lay out 4932 as place-value counters: 4 thousands, 9 hundreds, 3 tens, 2 ones.

Share each column left to right into 6 equal groups, starting with the thousands (4 thousands won't make a group of 6, so that place gives 0 — exchange the 4 thousands for 40 hundreds and carry them on).

When a column won't share evenly, exchange each leftover counter for ten counters of the next-lower place and add them to that column (e.g. a spare hundred becomes ten tens that join the tens column).
Record the quotient digit for each place above the bus-stop layout as you go, and write the carried amount beside the next digit.
When the divisor won't go into a place at all, write 0 in the quotient for that place and carry the whole amount onward — do not skip the place.
Finish with 4932 ÷ 6 = 822 and note there is no remainder here; then repeat with a dividend that leaves a remainder.
activities.insight: The 'carried remainder' of the written short-division method is the same idea as regrouping/exchanging place-value counters: a leftover in one column is worth ten of the next place down. Every place of the dividend produces a quotient digit, including a 0 when the divisor won't go.

activities.title: One division, three answers: interpreting the remainder in context
steps: Take a single division that leaves a remainder and solve it once — for example, 125 ÷ 8 = 15 remainder 5.

Read that SAME result (15 remainder 5) inside three different stories about 125 items: 'containers that each hold 8 — how many containers are needed for 125 items?' (round the quotient UP to 16, because the 5 left over still need a container), 'full bags of 8 — how many full bags from 125 sweets?' (round DOWN to 15, with 5 left over), and 'share 125 cm of ribbon fairly among 8 groups — how much each?' (the leftover can be split, so express it as a fraction, giving 15 and 5/8 cm each).
State in words what the leftover of 5 means in each story (e.g. '5 sweets are not enough to fill another full bag').
Decide, for each story, whether the right answer rounds up, rounds down, or keeps the remainder — and justify why.
For extra practice with the round-up case, try 52 children into minibuses of 9: 52 ÷ 9 = 5 remainder 7, which rounds UP to 6 minibuses because the 7 leftover children still need transport.
activities.insight: The same calculation gives different legitimate answers depending on what the leftover represents in the situation; interpreting the remainder is a decision about the context, not a fixed rule applied to the number.

activities.title: Estimate first, check by multiplying back
steps: Before dividing, make a rough estimate by rounding to friendly numbers (round 4932 to about 4800, then 4800 ÷ 6 = 800), so expect a quotient near 800 — about three figures. Avoid rounding the divisor down (e.g. 6 to 5), which would inflate the estimate.
Carry out the short division to get a quotient and any remainder.
Check with the inverse: compute quotient × divisor (+ remainder) and confirm it equals the dividend, e.g. 822 × 6 = 4932.
Compare the answer with the estimate and ask whether it is sensible; if the check fails, find and fix the slip rather than re-learning the method.
activities.insight: Division and multiplication are inverses: quotient × divisor (+ remainder) = dividend. An estimate and an inverse check catch arithmetic slips and keep the quotient's size reasonable.

activities.title: Talk it through: does the leftover change the answer?
steps: With a partner or guide, discuss a solved division in a real story: 'We have a remainder of 5 — do we need another minibus, or is 5 left over fine?'
Argue for rounding up or down and give the reason in terms of the story.
Explain to the other person what the remainder means and why the chosen answer fits the situation.
activities.insight: Deciding what to do with a remainder is a reasoned choice about the context that can be defended out loud, not an automatic operation.

checkQuestion: Ask the child to compute 4,932 ÷ 6 by short division while you watch, then 125 ÷ 8 and tell you what the remainder means if these were sweets going into bags of 8. Watch how they carry the remainder from one column to the next and whether they interpret the final remainder in context.
checkAnswer: 4,932 ÷ 6 = 822. 125 ÷ 8 = 15 remainder 5 (15 full bags, 5 sweets left over). The teacher watches for correct short-division bookkeeping — carrying the remainder into the next digit — and a sensible contextual reading of the final remainder.
